passage_text: Researchers studied the effect of a novel cognitive training program on reaction time among adults aged 25–35. Participants were randomly assigned to either the training group (n = 40) or a control group (n = 40) that received no intervention. Over a 4‑week period, reaction times were recorded weekly. The table below summarizes the mean reaction times (in milliseconds) and standard deviations for each group at each time point. The training group showed a progressive decrease in reaction time, suggesting improved processing speed, whereas the control group’s reaction times remained relatively stable. The study aimed to determine whether the training program could produce measurable cognitive benefits and to evaluate the magnitude of change over time.
stem: Which of the following best describes the trend observed in the training group’s reaction times across the 4-week period?

options.D: Reaction times fluctuated without a clear pattern.

explanation: The mean reaction time for the training group decreased from 520 ms in week 1 to 455 ms in week 4, indicating a steady improvement in processing speed.
trap: A common misinterpretation is to focus on the control group’s stable values and conclude that no change occurred overall.

stem: Which variable did the researchers manipulate by random assignment?
explanation: Correct: C) Participants were randomly assigned to training or control, so group assignment is the manipulated variable. Why the others are wrong: A) Mean reaction time is the measured outcome. B) The standard deviation is a descriptive statistic of the outcome. D) Week is the measurement time point and was not assigned to participants.
trap: Choosing reaction time as the manipulated variable; it is the measured outcome, whereas the group to which participants were assigned is what the researchers controlled.

stem: What was the percent reduction in the training group's mean reaction time from week 1 to week 4?
explanation: Correct: D) (520 - 455)/520 x 100 = 12.5%. Why the others are wrong: A) 0.6% is the control group's change (518 to 515, 3/518). B) 9.6% uses the week 1 to week 3 change (50/520). C) 14.3% divides the 65 ms change by the final value (455) instead of the baseline.
trap: Dividing the change by the final value (65/455 = 14.3%) instead of the week 1 baseline, or using the control group's tiny change.

stem: Which statement is best supported by the table and the described design?

options.A: The training program was more effective than a placebo program.
options.B: Mean reaction time fell by 65 ms in the training group and by 3 ms in the control group between week 1 and week 4.
options.C: The reaction-time gains will persist after training stops.
options.D: The training program improves cognitive function in all adults.

explanation: Correct: B) Training: 520 - 455 = 65 ms; control: 518 - 515 = 3 ms. Why the others are wrong: A) The control group received no intervention, so no placebo comparison was made. C) Nothing was measured after training ended. D) Only adults aged 25-35 were studied, and only reaction time was measured.
trap: Treating a no-intervention control as a placebo control, or generalizing beyond the sample, instead of sticking to the changes shown in the table.

stem: At week 4, how much faster was the training group's mean reaction time than the control group's?
explanation: Correct: C) Week 4 means: control 515 ms, training 455 ms, a 60 ms difference. Why the others are wrong: A) 3 ms is the control group's own change from week 1 to week 4. B) 45 ms is the training group's week 1 SD, not a between-group difference. D) 65 ms is the training group's own change from week 1 to week 4, not a comparison with control.
trap: Reporting the training group's own improvement (65 ms) rather than the week 4 difference between the two groups.
